name: Hold the CPU clocks while benchmarking

atomicDiscipline.rule: Run exactly the printed hypothesis. If the attempted change fails, degrades, or suggests a different fix, revert to the checkpoint and finish this experiment as failure. Start a new experiment for the next idea.

hypothesisMarkdown: The +21% CPU of scroll-data-table and dashboard-one-panel with fast mode on against the opening state is not more work. A bisect over six kept commits showed no single step and no regression for dashboard-one-panel at all, the sample profile of the 'slower' build held fewer main-thread samples than the faster one (857 against 1,048), and main_cpu_ms is thread CPU time, which grows when the core runs at a lower clock for lighter frames.
measurementPlanMarkdown: Run the opening binary and the final binary alternated with three busy processes beside them so the clusters stay clocked up, over all 15 scenarios, fast off and on, 3 repetitions. Add a --hold-clocks option to run.py so the benchmark can do it and document the caveat.

measurements.metric: scroll-data-table fast on CPU (clocks idle > held)
geometric mean CPU over 15 scenarios, fast off / on
geometric mean Window::draw p50, fast off / on

reportMarkdown: With the clocks held every scenario improved against the opening state and none regressed; the earlier idle-clock comparison understated the gains and invented two regressions. The same main-thread work read 2.9 ms idle and 1.0 ms held on the data table. run.py gained --hold-clocks N (busy processes for the desktop runs, recorded in meta.json), tested end to end, and the README documents the caveat. The changelog and the memory rules are corrected.
decisionMarkdown: Keep. No product code changed: the 'regressions' were a measurement artifact, and the fix is the measurement.
